Plan Sample Size to Make the Test of the Squared Multiple Correlation Coefficient Sufficiently Powerful

Source: R/ss_power_R2.R
ss_power_R2.Rd

Determine the necessary sample size for the omnibus test of the squared multiple correlation coefficient (\(R^2\)), or the realized statistical power given a specified sample size, under either fixed or random predictors. The fixed-predictors path uses Cohen's (1988) noncentral F formulation; the random-predictors path uses the three-moment noncentral F approximation of Lee (1971, Section 5.1) to the sampling distribution of the sample \(R^2\) under joint multivariate normality.

Usage

ss_power_R2(
  true_R2 = NULL,
  alpha_level = 0.05,
  desired_power = 0.85,
  p,
  specified_N = NULL,
  true_f2 = NULL,
  null_R2 = 0,
  random_predictors = TRUE,
  print_iter = FALSE
)

Arguments

true_R2

Population squared multiple correlation coefficient the sample size or power is planned for. The planner treats this value as the truth; ss_power_R2_sensitivity shows what the plan delivers when the truth (true_R2 there) differs from the value planned with (supposed_R2 there).

alpha_level

Type I error rate

desired_power

Desired degree of statistical power, a single number strictly between 0 and 1. The values 0 and 1 are refused, with a condition of class dmar_desired_power_invalid.

p

The number of predictor variables

specified_N

The sample size used to calculate power (rather than determine necessary sample size). This is the total sample size across all groups or observations.

true_f2

Cohen's (1988) effect size for multiple regression: true_R2/(1 - true_R2).

null_R2

The null value of the omnibus test, which must be 0. Any other value stops with an error of class dmar_null_R2_unsupported that explains why and gives the call to ss_power_R2_change; see Details.

random_predictors

Whether the predictor variables are treated as random (TRUE, the default) or fixed (FALSE). See Details.

print_iter

If the progress of the iterative procedure is printed to the screen as the iterations are occurring

Value

A data.frame with columns term and value. For an \(N\) search the rows are necessary_N, actual_power, noncentral_f_parm (only meaningful for random_predictors = FALSE; NA otherwise), and true_f2 (Cohen's \(f^2 = \rho^2 / (1 - \rho^2)\) at true_R2). For a power-at-specified-N computation the first row is specified_N instead of necessary_N.

Details

Determine the necessary sample size given a particular true_R2, alpha_level, p, and desired_power. Alternatively, given true_R2, alpha_level, p, and specified_N, the function can be used to determine the statistical power.

Fixed vs.\ random predictors. The two regression models give different sampling distributions for the omnibus \(F\)-statistic, and so different power. Under fixed predictors the design matrix is treated as constant in hypothetical replications of the study, and \(F\) follows a noncentral F with \(p\) and \(N-p-1\) degrees of freedom and noncentrality \(\lambda = N \cdot f^2\), where \(f^2 = \rho^2 / (1 - \rho^2)\) and \(\rho^2\) is true_R2 (Cohen, 1988). Cohen's noncentrality is \(\lambda = f^2 (u + v + 1)\), with \(u\) and \(v\) the numerator and denominator degrees of freedom (as given by Maxwell, 2000, Equation 1); for the omnibus test \(u = p\) and \(v = N - p - 1\), so \(u + v + 1 = N\) and the two forms are the same. Under random predictors the design matrix is itself a draw from a joint multivariate normal distribution, and the unconditional distribution of the sample \(R^2\) is due to Fisher (1928); ss_power_R2() uses the three-moment noncentral F approximation of Lee (1971, Section 5.1) to that distribution, the same approximation ci_R2() uses for random-predictor confidence intervals. Gatsonis and Sampson (1989) give the exact calculation for random predictors and compare it with Cohen's tables (the 1977 edition of the book cited below), whose sample sizes were slightly smaller than the exact ones for most designs with up to 10 predictors. The sample size this function returns under random predictors is the smallest at which the power by Lee's approximation attains desired_power. Against the exact distribution, the power by Lee's approximation differed by at most .0043 over the combinations examined (squared correlations up to .95, alpha_level from .001 to .10, and one or more error degrees of freedom) and by at most .0004 with 25 or more error degrees of freedom; the necessary sample size differed from the one the exact distribution gives, by one case, in 20 of 1,500 searches, and in those the power by the exact distribution at the size returned was within .0011 of desired_power. In the behavioral, educational, and social sciences predictor variables are almost always random, so the default is random_predictors = TRUE; pass random_predictors = FALSE for designs in which the predictor variables are fixed by design (for example, planned dosing levels).

Tests other than the omnibus test. ss_power_R2() plans the test that the population squared multiple correlation coefficient of all p predictors is zero. The test that predictors added to a model contribute nothing, a test of the change in \(R^2\), is planned with ss_power_R2_change, which takes the number of predictors in both models.

null_R2 exists so that a call written for MBESS with a nonzero null value is answered with an explanation; it must be 0. A nonzero value stops with an error of class dmar_null_R2_unsupported (see dmar_metadata), for these reasons. In MBESS a nonzero null value \(\rho_0^2\) forms the effect size \((\rho^2 - \rho_0^2) / (1 - \rho^2)\), which is Cohen's (1988) \(f^2\) for the increment in \(R^2\) when predictors are added to a model that already explains \(\rho_0^2\), and refers it to an F distribution with \(p\) and \(N - p - 1\) degrees of freedom and noncentrality \(N f^2\). What that calculation is depends on how p is read. With p read as the number of predictors added, it is Cohen's calculation, \(\lambda = f^2 (u + v + 1)\), for a study whose total sample size is \(N\) plus the number of predictors in the restricted model: the sample size it reports is Cohen's total sample size less that number. With p read as all of the predictors, as this function defines it, the calculation is not the test of the increment, whose numerator degrees of freedom are the number of predictors added and not p. The argument alone cannot say which calculation is meant, because the test of an increment needs the number of predictors in the restricted model, so the value is refused and the message writes the call to ss_power_R2_change().

The number that MBESS returns for a population value \(a\) and a null value \(b\) is ss_power_R2(true_f2 = (a - b) / (1 - a), p = p, random_predictors = FALSE), the omnibus test of p predictors with an effect of that size; the last example shows it. Whether the population squared multiple correlation coefficient of all p predictors exceeds a stated value above zero is a third question. DMAR does not plan sample size for that test; the test itself rejects when the one-sided lower confidence limit from ci_R2 (with alpha_lower = alpha_level and alpha_upper = 0) exceeds the stated value.

Limit of the calculation. R computes the noncentral F distribution accurately for a noncentrality parameter up to about one million, and warns beyond it. ss_power_R2() returns no power from an evaluation at which R gave that warning: a power requested at such a specified_N is refused, and a search whose answer lies there stops and says so. A search that only passes through such sizes on its way to a smaller answer returns that answer, which is evaluated without the warning. The search does not go beyond a sample size of ten million, and stops with an error when desired_power is not attained by then. With true_R2 of 0 the null hypothesis is true: the power at a specified_N is alpha_level, and a search stops with an error of class dmar_effect_zero because no sample size attains desired_power.

Note

When determining sample size for a desired degree of power, there will always be a slightly larger degree of actual power. This is the case because the algorithm employed determines sample size until the actual power is no less than the desired power (given sample size is a whole number power will almost certainly not be exactly the specified value). This is the same as other statistical power procedures that return whole numbers for necessary sample size.

References

Cohen, J. (1988). Statistical power analysis for the behavioral sciences (2nd ed.). Hillsdale, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum.

Fisher, R. A. (1928). The general sampling distribution of the multiple correlation coefficient. Proceedings of the Royal Society of London, Series A, 121(788), 654–673. doi:10.1098/rspa.1928.0224

Gatsonis, C., & Sampson, A. R. (1989). Multiple correlation: Exact power and sample size calculations. Psychological Bulletin, 106(3), 516–524.

Kelley, K., & Maxwell, S. E. (2003). Sample size for multiple regression: Obtaining regression coefficients that are accurate, not simply significant. Psychological Methods, 8(3), 305–321. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.8.3.305

Kelley, K. (2008). Sample size planning for the squared multiple correlation coefficient: Accuracy in parameter estimation via narrow confidence intervals. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 43(4), 524–555. doi:10.1080/00273170802490632

Kelley, K., & Maxwell, S. E. (2008). Sample size planning with applications to multiple regression: Power and accuracy for omnibus and targeted effects. In P. Alasuutari, L. Bickman, & J. Brannen (Eds.), The Sage handbook of social research methods (pp. 166–192). Sage.

Lee, Y. S. (1971). Some results on the sampling distribution of the multiple correlation coefficient. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 33(1), 117–130.

Maxwell, S. E. (2000). Sample size and multiple regression analysis. Psychological Methods, 5(4), 434–458. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.5.4.434

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge. (See Chapter 3 on \(R^2\) as a model comparison effect size.)

Maxwell, S. E., Kelley, K., & Rausch, J. R. (2008). Sample size planning for statistical power and accuracy in parameter estimation. Annual Review of Psychology, 59, 537–563. doi:10.1146/annurev.psych.59.103006.093735

Anderson, S. F., Kelley, K., & Maxwell, S. E. (2017). Sample-size planning for more accurate statistical power: A method adjusting sample effect sizes for publication bias and uncertainty. Psychological Science, 28(11), 1547–1562. doi:10.1177/0956797617723724

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# Random predictors (default; appropriate for most behavioral / social
# science applications).
ss_power_R2(true_R2 = .5, alpha_level = .05, desired_power = .85, p = 5)
#>  term              value
#>  necessary_N       23   
#>  actual_power      0.852
#>  noncentral_f_parm <NA> 
#>  true_f2           1    

# Fixed predictors (Cohen 1988): predictor variables fixed by design.
ss_power_R2(true_R2 = .5, alpha_level = .05, desired_power = .85,
            p = 5, random_predictors = FALSE)
#>  term              value 
#>  necessary_N       21    
#>  actual_power      0.858 
#>  noncentral_f_parm 21.000
#>  true_f2           1     

# Effect size input (Cohen's f^2).
ss_power_R2(true_f2 = 1, alpha_level = .05, desired_power = .85, p = 5)
#>  term              value
#>  necessary_N       23   
#>  actual_power      0.852
#>  noncentral_f_parm <NA> 
#>  true_f2           1    

# Realized power at a specified N.
ss_power_R2(true_R2 = .5, specified_N = 15, alpha_level = .05,
            desired_power = .85, p = 5)
#>  term              value
#>  specified_N       15   
#>  actual_power      0.543
#>  noncentral_f_parm <NA> 
#>  true_f2           1    

# The number MBESS reported for a population value of .30 against a null
# value of .25 with p = 4: the omnibus test of four fixed predictors with
# Cohen's f squared for that increment. The test of the increment itself
# is planned with ss_power_R2_change().
ss_power_R2(true_f2 = (.30 - .25) / (1 - .30), p = 4, specified_N = 85,
            alpha_level = .01, random_predictors = FALSE)
#>  term              value
#>  specified_N       85   
#>  actual_power      0.223
#>  noncentral_f_parm 6.071
#>  true_f2           0.071
